Question: What is holding back India's progress?
Old_Answer: There is interesting news today published in all leading newspapers of India. According to a recent study conducted by the Indian Veterinary Research Institute, India's premier animal research body, ‘cow urine contains at least 14 types of harmful bacteria, including those commonly associated with stomach infections in humans. The study contradicts existing beliefs about the antibacterial properties of cow urine and highlights that it cannot be recommended for human consumption.[1] I did not find anything surprising in the research because I know that if there be an iota of truth in the medical utility of cow urine, scientists worldwide would have been using cow urine for treating various diseases. However, I am very sure that millions of Indians, including highly educated ones, would dismiss such research, and continue to believe that cow urine is nothing less than a miraculous medicine. People believe in the miraculous properties of cow urine because according to Ayurveda, Gomutra (cow urine) can cure leprosy, fevers, peptic ulcers, liver ailments, kidney disorders, asthma, certain allergies, psoriasis, anaemia and even cancer.[2] Since something is written in the holy book of Ayurveda, how can it be wrong? Many top Indian leaders keep advocating the use of cow urine for cure of any ailment, including COvid-19 virus. For example, some time ago, West Bengal BJP president Dilip Ghosh advocated the use of “cow-urine” to boost immunity in the fight against COVID-19. [3] Similarly, BJP MP Pragya Thakur claimed that cow urine can cure lung infection caused by Coronavirus, adding she is protected from the virus as she takes cow urine every day. She told a party gathering sometime ago, “If we have desi gau mutra (urine from an indigenous cow)[how nationalistic!] every day then it cures lung infection from Covid. I am in deep pain but I take cow urine every day. So, now I don’t have to take any medicine against corona and I don't have corona.”[4] The Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan even claimed: “cows, cow-dung and its urine can help strengthen the economy of the state and entire nation if a proper system is put in place”. The most unfortunate thing about most Indians is that they have little faith in scientific study and more faith in the words of their leaders (religious and political) and the ancient scriptures. There are millions of such myths, which are totally false and unscientific, and still, hundreds of millions Indians believe in such lies. Unless Indians learn to think rationally, develop a scientific temper, and stop believing in mythologies, India can never become a happy, developed and prosperous nation.

Question: What are the reasons for the existence of corruption in some countries like India and Pakistan, while countries like Singapore and Japan have lower levels of corruption? Is it accurate to say that there is no corruption at all in Singapore and Japan?
Old_Answer: Corruption has a negative correlation with development and economic prosperity. According to Transparency International, the list of the least and most corrupt countries in the world as of 2023 is as follows, [1] The least corrupt countries in the world The most corrupt countries in the world You can easily see that without an exception, all the least corrupt countries are the developed countries with a per capita income of $20,000 or more. Similarly, the most corrupt countries of the world are also the least developed countries whose per capita income is hardly $2000. The position of India was 93 with a CPI score of 39/100 in 2023, while that of Pakistan is 133 with a CPI Score of 29/100 in 2023. Thus, India and Pakistan are in the middle of the list of corrupt countries. Hence, it is evident that corruption can’t be removed unless the country achieves economic prosperity and becomes a developed country. Singapore and Japan are the most honest countries in Asia because they are also the most developed countries in Asia. None of the countries in the world is free from corruption, as no country has a CPI score of 10/10. The CPI scores of Singapore and Japan are 83/100 and 73/100, respectively, which means that corruption is less in these countries than in India (39/100), but these countries are still not free from corruption. Corruption and poverty are thus positively correlated Hence, it is unrealistic to assume that a country can become honest without achieving development. Since economic development is a slow process, the reduction of corruption is also a slow process. However, corruption must naturally reduce as the national economy improves and the country's per capita income rises. Unfortunately, that is not happening in India, at least after 2016. The ranking of India in 2023 was 93 (CPI 39/100), while it was 80 in 2016 (CPI 40/100), while in the same period, the per capita income of India increased from $1714 (2016) to $2411 (2022)[2]. Thus, corruption in India is increasing despite economic development due to the patronising of corruption by the elected governments in India, who have politicised and reduced the power of the anti-corruption agencies. The following data show that India's CPI score was constantly improving prior to 2016, and there was a significant improvement in the period 2012–2014[3] because, in those days, the anti-corruption agencies had more freedom to do their jobs and could arrest even the ruling party politicians and central ministers without seeking approval from the government. Since more corruption cases were booked and freely reported earlier, the popular perception then was that corruption was increasing 2012-2015. However, after 2018, when corruption actually started increasing due to amendment of Prevention of Corruption Act curbing the powers of anti-corruption agencies, the Indian public is under the impression that it is going down because corruption cases against the ruling parties are not started and not reported.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Corruption is a complex phenomenon influenced by various socio-economic, political, and cultural factors. In countries like India and Pakistan, corruption often thrives due to a combination of weak institutions, lack of accountability, and a culture that sometimes normalizes unethical behavior. The bureaucratic systems in these nations can be cumbersome, leading to opportunities for bribery and favoritism as individuals seek to navigate red tape. Additionally, the socio-economic disparities create an environment where corruption becomes a means of survival for many. In contrast, countries like Singapore and Japan have established strong institutions, transparent governance, and a culture of accountability that discourages corrupt practices. Their legal frameworks are robust, and there is a societal expectation for integrity, which significantly reduces the scope for corruption. However, it would be misleading to claim that there is no corruption at all in Singapore and Japan. While the levels are considerably lower, instances of corruption do exist, albeit at a much smaller scale and often dealt with swiftly by the authorities. The key difference lies in the systemic approach to governance and the societal values that prioritize ethical behavior over personal gain. Thus, while corruption may be less visible in these countries, it is not entirely absent; rather, it is managed more effectively, reflecting the importance of institutional integrity and cultural attitudes towards corruption.
Answer_with_user_profile: Corruption is a multifaceted issue that often stems from a combination of historical, cultural, and socio-economic factors. In countries like India and Pakistan, corruption can be attributed to a legacy of colonial rule, where systems were established that favored a select few, leading to entrenched practices of bribery and nepotism. Additionally, the lack of transparency and accountability in governance, coupled with weak institutions, creates an environment where corrupt practices can thrive. In contrast, countries like Singapore and Japan have implemented robust legal frameworks, strong institutions, and a culture of accountability that discourages corruption. The key difference lies in how these countries address and manage corruption when it arises, with stringent laws and a societal expectation of ethical behavior. Thus, while the presence of corruption may vary, the effectiveness of governance and societal norms play a critical role in shaping the corruption landscape in any nation.

The key difference lies in how these countries manage and mitigate corruption through stringent regulations, public awareness, and a culture of civic responsibility. Thus, while corruption may be less visible in Singapore and Japan, it is not entirely absent; rather, it is effectively contained, demonstrating that the fight against corruption requires continuous effort and commitment from both the government and the citizens.

Question: Is India ready for a uniform civil code? What would be the benefits in eliminating religious personal laws? Are the concerns against it justified?
Old_Answer: The recent statement of Indian Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi that India needed a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) as the country could not run with the dual system of “separate laws for separate communities”, has fuelled speculation for the implementation of Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in India soon. UCC has been in the manifesto of the BJP for a long time and with Modi Government commanding a majority in Parliament, there is a high possibility of UCC law being passed soon. The Uniform Civil Code means that the same law shall be applicable to all uniformly in matters of - Marriage, divorce, maintenance, inheritance, adoption and succession of property, irrespective of religion. The term, ‘Uniform Civil Code’ is explicitly mentioned in Article 44 of the Indian Constitution, which says “The State shall endeavor to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” In my opinion, UCC is good for the country as it will be in the spirit of secular India where people shall be given equal status irrespective of their religion. Objections against UCC Since UCC shall be dealing with issues like marriage, divorce, maintenance etc, which have been traditionally decided on the basis of religion, the detractors would contend that it will rob the nation of its religious diversity and violate the fundamental right to practise religion enshrined in Article 25 and Article 29 of the Constitution. They argue that UCC is a directive principle which can’t override the fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution. Article 25 provides the freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion, while Article 29 provides that all sections of the citizens having a distinct language, script or culture of their own shall have the right to conserve the same. However, I believe that many cultures and traditions have outdated and must be discarded as soon as possible to create a modern society. For example, there is no provision for divorce and property inheritance by daughters in the Hindu religion. However, Indian laws have been implemented to provide these rights to Hindu women. In Islam, there is a provision that men can marry up to four women. Similarly, divorce provisions are much easier in Islam, and even triple talaq is permitted. Further, under Muslim personal law, maintenance was to be paid only till the period of iddat. (three lunar months-roughly 90 days ).[1] Way Ahead I don’t think that any right-minded person would support the right of a man to have four wives. The very concept appears repugnant to me, which denies dignity to women in the modern world. I also believe that women of all religions must be equally protected from arbitrary divorce and given the same compensation which can ensure them a dignified life. Surely, there will be opposition to the UCC by some people and political parties to influence their vote bank. Yet, the opponents of UCC would be in small numbers in India and those who oppose UCC may pay a heavy price for opposing this progressive move by Government. However, the drafting of UCC must be done very carefully incorporating the best practices of all religions so that no religion feels discriminated against or privileged.

The lack of stringent accountability mechanisms allows corrupt practices to flourish. Moreover, the political landscape is often dominated by a culture of patronage and nepotism, where loyalty to party lines supersedes ethical governance. This environment fosters a sense of impunity, as many politicians believe they can act without fear of repercussions. As long as the incentives for corruption outweigh the consequences, and as long as the electorate remains passive, we will continue to witness the emergence of corrupt politicians. It is crucial for society to demand transparency, hold leaders accountable, and actively participate in the democratic process to break this cycle and foster a culture of integrity in politics.

Question: Why did Hindutva not work well this time for BJP & Modi? Is it due to new found unity among the opposition parties or did the low percentage of voting as such helped the I.N.D.I.A?
Old_Answer: “You can fool some of the people all of the time and all of the people some of the time, but you can not fool all of the people all of the time.” This famous quote from Abraham Lincoln explains the defeat of the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. The Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanathsaid claimed before the election that the Samajwadi Party (SP) would fail to open its account in the 2024 Lok Sabha election and that all the five members of the party’s first family were set to lose.[1] However, after the election, BJP has to eat the humble pie. Not only did SP open its account and won 37 seats, and its alliance partner Congress, won 6 seats, but the tally of BJP was reduced to less than half at merely 33 seats in UP.[2] They even lost in Ayodhya. This happened when the BSP was not part of the INDIA alliance. If the BSP had joined the INDIA alliance, the BJP's performance would have been even worse. It is apparent that the Hindutva card played by the BJP has outlived its utility, and Hindus can’t vote for the BJP merely on the issue of Hindutva or Ram Mandir. The BJP's national vote share fell from 37.3 percent in 2019 to 36.6 percent in 2024, which is not very significant. But, the BJP lost 63 seats (from 303 to 240), because the INDIA alliance helped consolidate the opposition votes in many places. [3] This happened when opposition parties were not fully united, and their votes split in most parts of India. Thus, it is evident that if opposition parties are united, the BJP has no chance of winning a majority in the Parliament. The BJP’s success has been largely due to its divide-and-rule strategy, which divided the Indians on a communal basis and ensured that the opposition parties didn’t come together by using the ED, CBI, and Income Tax departments. While Modi has become the PM for the third time, the interesting thing is that this time, it is the NDA government in the centre and not the Modi Government, where Modi enjoyed absolute power due to his absolute majority in parliament. I hope the results of the 2024 elections will bring some sanity to the rank and files of the BJP and Shri Modi and make them respect the opinions and ideologies of more than 63% of Indians who have not voted for them as they don’t accept their Hindutva agenda in politics.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The recent electoral performance of the BJP and Modi, despite their strong Hindutva narrative, can be attributed to a confluence of factors rather than a singular cause. Firstly, the opposition's newfound unity under the I.N.D.I.A. coalition has created a formidable front that resonates with a diverse electorate, countering the BJP's divisive tactics. This unity has not only consolidated votes but also instilled a sense of hope among those disillusioned by the ruling party's governance. Secondly, the low voter turnout reflects a growing apathy among the electorate, particularly among the youth and urban voters who once formed the BJP's core support base. This disengagement can be seen as a response to the perceived failures of the government in addressing pressing issues such as unemployment, inflation, and social unrest. Moreover, the Hindutva ideology, while potent, may have alienated moderate voters who prioritize economic stability and social harmony over religious nationalism. The BJP's reliance on Hindutva as a political strategy may have backfired, as it failed to address the immediate concerns of the populace. In essence, the interplay of a united opposition and a disenchanted electorate has significantly undermined the effectiveness of Hindutva, revealing that political narratives must evolve to remain relevant in a dynamic socio-political landscape.

The Hindutva narrative, while powerful, must evolve to resonate with the contemporary aspirations of the populace, or it risks becoming an outdated relic in the face of a more pragmatic electorate.

Question: Is it possible for a person to completely change their habits in an instant?
Old_Answer: I was a good student in my school days. I was not the best, as used to stand second or third in the class, but I was very righteous as I neither copied, nor liked anyone else to copy in the examination. I hated the very idea of copying and cheating in the examination because that was against the sincere student who may end up scoring lesser marks despite their hard work and superior knowledge while the cheaters can get better marks by copying. Hence, when I found someone cheating in the examination hall, I would often complain against the person to the examiner, though it angered the cheaters. When I joined my B Tech (Mechanical Engineering), in IIT-BHU (Then known as IT-BHU) Varanasi, during the internal tests, most professors allowed us the freedom to choose our seats, while in the end-semester examination, everyone was required to sit on the seats according to their roll numbers. It was fashionable for the students to occupy the seats from the last rows, where the examiner couldn’t see the students clearly, and hence one could copy the answers from the neighbour answer sheet. Since I had no intention to cheat, I used to occupy the first-row seat in the class, while my friends preferred the last seats. Some of these students scored better grades than me despite studying much lesser, and they used to laugh at me for being honest. Since these people were in large numbers and I had to live with them in the same hostel, I did not wish to antagonise them by complaining against them. So, what did I do? I followed the dictum, “If you can't beat them, join them.” One of my friends convinced me of the benefit of cheating in the examination, “Awdhesh! Copying does not mean that you stop studying. Question: Richard Feynman said, “Never confuse education with intelligence, you can have a PhD and still be an idiot.” What are some real life examples of this?
Old_Answer: Intelligence is generally defined as the ability to gather knowledge and skills and apply them to your life to solve life's complex problems. On the other hand, education requires you to get into a college and pass the examination prescribed by law to get the required degree. If you have a good memory and follow rote learning, you can easily get even the highest degree in the world with top marks. Getting a degree has become so easy in modern times that anyone with average intelligence can acquire any degree, including a PhD, provided he or she is willing to spend the desired time pursuing the degree. Most PhD holders work in universities, where a PhD is the minimum requirement to become a faculty member. However, many professors are people of average intelligence who often choose the teaching profession not as a matter of choice but because they did not get into the best jobs at their lower qualifications. Smarter people often get jobs after their BE/B Tech, MBA, LLB/LLM, MBBS/MS, etc., and have better career prospects. The wisest people in the world, like Buddha, Kabir, or Socrates did not have a college degree, but they learned their lessons from life itself using their analytical skills and keen observation. While education is helpful in acquiring knowledge, it does not make you more intelligent. Knowledge acquired from textbooks can make an intelligent person wiser and more creative, but it can also make a stupid person even more stupid. The story of ‘Four Learned Fools’ from Panchtantra illustrates how education can’t make a stupid person intelligent. In a town, there lived four friends who were quite learned. One day, they decided to leave their native place and seek their fortune in the city, which offered so many more opportunities to earn money. Packing in all their holy books, they were on their way.[1] Soon, they came to an intersection of the road and did not know which path to follow. Now, the son of a merchant had died in the town, and at that very moment, a huge funeral procession that included several prominent citizens of the town passed by. One of the friends consulted his holy scriptures and read aloud: ‘Whichever road is followed by great men is the right one to follow’. So they said, ‘Let us go the same way as these people.’ Following the road taken by the prominent citizens, the group reached the cremation ground, and saw a donkey standing there. The second friend opened his holy scriptures and read: ‘Whosoever stands by you on all occasions, whether joyous or sad, is your true friend’. So, the four friends concluded that the donkey was their true friend. Accordingly, one of the friends put his arms around the donkey’s neck; the second friend kissed him, whilst the third began to wash his hoofs. They kept chanting, ‘He is our true friend’. Just then, they saw a camel advance quickly towards them. The third friend consulted his religious book and read: ‘Righteousness marches rapidly.’ So they all agreed that the advancing camel must be nothing but righteousness incarnate. Right then, the fourth friend opened his holy scriptures and read: ‘A wise man should lead his friend to righteousness’. So they decided to introduce the donkey to the camel, and when the camel approached, they tied the two animals together. When the donkey’s master, a washerman, heard the news that his donkey was being dragged along by a camel, he picked up a stick to beat the four learned fools, who then had to run for their lives. When they had gone a little way, the foursome came upon a river. The leaf of a holy tree was floating by. One of them cried, ‘This holy leaf will take us across the river.’ And with this, he jumped on it and immediately began to drown. Then, another friend caught him by the neck. However, the friend recalled certain words of wisdom: ‘When total destruction is imminent, a wise man sacrifices half and works with the rest.’ So he concluded, ‘He should be cut into two!’ And they cut the friend they had saved into two halves with a sharp sword and moved on. [2] It is easy to see that these learned fools had all the right knowledge, but they did not know how to use it correctly to solve real-life problems. So, Richard Feynman is right. A highly educated person can be stupid because education makes an intelligent person smarter, but a stupid person a bigger idiot.
